2027-05-01.title: Fifth Saturday of Resurrection · St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class

2027-05-01.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The First Set calendar lists St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class, on 1 May with the readings above (verify locally whether your parish keeps the feast readings). Weekday readings of the Fifth Saturday of Resurrection: Hebrews 7:11–17; John 15:26–16:4. In the Latin calendar St Joseph the Worker is an optional memorial, placed on 1 May by Pope Pius XII in 1955. Today is also May Day, Labour Day, and the first day of the month that our families dedicate to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-01.verse: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
theo: On the first day of May, when many nations honour working men and women, the Church turns to a working man of Nazareth. In 1955 Pope Pius XII placed a feast of St Joseph the Worker on this day, so that the workers of the world would have a patron and a model, and so that no one would think that the Church looks on labour from a distance. Our Syro-Malabar families know Joseph well. We call him Yauseppithavu, Father Joseph; we keep March as his month and Wednesday as his day; countless churches in Kerala bear his name, and many a family begins a new house or a new business with a prayer to him. Today's Gospel gives him the only title the people of Nazareth ever gave him: the carpenter. The word used in Matthew's Greek, tekton, means a craftsman, a builder who worked with wood and perhaps with stone, making ploughs and yokes, doors and roof beams for the village. Mark's Gospel gives the same title to Jesus himself: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mark 6:3). For about thirty years the Son of God lived in that workshop, learned the trade from Joseph, and earned his bread as the people around him did. The Church sees in this hidden life a great teaching: the greater part of the Saviour's life on earth was spent in ordinary work (Catechism 531–533).

The first reading takes us back to the beginning, to the words spoken to Adam after the first sin: “cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life”, and “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Then the man is sent out of the garden “to till the ground from which he was taken.” It would be easy to conclude that work itself is a punishment. Scripture says otherwise. Before there was any sin, “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work belonged to God's first plan for us; it is a share in his own care for creation. What sin brought was the thorns and thistles, the toil that wears us out, the sweat, the frustration, the work that seems never to bear fruit. The good news of Nazareth is that the Son of God entered into exactly this toil. The Second Vatican Council says that he worked with human hands and thought with a human mind (Gaudium et Spes 22). In the workshop of Joseph, sweat itself was taken up into the work of redemption. The farmer in Kuttanad, the woman at the tea estate in Munnar, the young nurse on a night shift in a hospital far from home: their sweat is not wasted when it is joined to his.

The second reading is the prayer of a king who knows that power and cleverness are not enough. Solomon asks God: “Send her forth from the holy heavens, and from the throne of your glory send her, that she may labor at my side, and that I may learn what is pleasing to you.” He admits frankly, “For the reasoning of mortals is worthless, and our designs are likely to fail”, and asks, “Who has learned your counsel, unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit from on high?” Joseph was such a man of wisdom, though he never sat on a throne. The Gospels do not record a single word from him; they record his obedience. Four times God spoke to him in a dream, and each time he rose and did what he was told: he took Mary as his wife, he fled with the child to Egypt, he returned, he settled in Nazareth (Matthew 1:20–24; 2:13–23). His wisdom was not a theory; it laboured at his side. In these last days before the Ascension and Pentecost, Solomon's prayer is the prayer of the whole Church: send your holy spirit from on high. Colossians tells us what such wisdom looks like in a household: “Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony”, and, “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.” That one verse could be written over the door of the house at Nazareth, and over the door of every Christian home and workplace.

In the Gospel Jesus comes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up are astounded: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?” Familiarity blinds them; “they took offense at him.” Jesus answers, “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house”, and Matthew adds a sad line: “he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.” Without knowing it, the villagers paid Joseph his greatest honour: the One who stood before them had been known for years simply as his son. The weekday readings of this Fifth Saturday complete the picture. Hebrews says that Jesus, born of the tribe of Judah and not of the priestly tribe, is a priest “through the power of an indestructible life”; the carpenter's son is the eternal high priest who offers himself for us. And in John Jesus promises, “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, he will testify on my behalf.” On this May Day we also remember the Church's long teaching on the dignity of work, from Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891) to St John Paul II's Laborem Exercens (1981), which says that work is for the human person, and not the person for work. We pray for those who have no work, for those who are paid unjustly, for the many workers from other states who build our houses in Kerala far from their families, and for our own sons and daughters who labour in the Gulf and across the world. St Joseph, patron of workers, pray for them all.
conn: To till it and keep it.
Before any sin, “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15): work is part of God's first plan.
Mark gives the title to Jesus himself: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mark 6:3).
Paul worked with his hands as a tentmaker at Corinth (Acts 18:3) and wrote: “Anyone unwilling to work should not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
Jesus calls all who toil: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
“Listen! The wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out” (James 5:4).
Hebrews 7:17 quotes Psalm 110:4: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”
altar: At the offertory of the Holy Qurbana the priest places on the altar bread and wine, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands”, as the Latin liturgy says. In them we offer our own week of labour, and the Lord who worked at Joseph's bench takes it up into his sacrifice.
The hands that made ploughs in Nazareth were nailed to the Cross and now bless us from the altar. Every Qurbana makes holy the work we bring to it.
outline: May Day and the carpenter of Nazareth.
Point 1 · By the sweat of your face
Work in God's first plan, toil after the fall, and toil redeemed.
Point 2 · Wisdom that labours at my side
Solomon's prayer and Joseph's silent obedience.
Point 3 · Is not this the carpenter's son?
The hidden years, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.
A father in Kerala closing his workshop at dusk and making the sign of the Cross before he goes home.
“Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
live: Begin your work today with a short prayer: Lord Jesus, I do this in your name.
If anyone works for you, at home or in business, make sure their wage is fair and paid on time.
Pray for those who labour far away
Pray today for one person you know who works far from home, in another state or abroad, and send them a message.
Begin the Marian month today with a decade of the Rosary at home, remembering the Holy Family at Nazareth.
fathers: Speaking of Paul, who sewed tents with his own hands, he says: let no one be ashamed of manual work. The apostle who preached to the nations was not ashamed to sit at the workbench. It is idleness that is disgraceful, not labour; work is a teacher of virtue.

In his hymns on the Nativity he imagines Joseph with the child: Joseph held the Son as a little one and served him as God; he rejoiced in him as the Good One and stood in awe before him as the Just One.
magis: During the greater part of his life Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of human beings: a daily life spent without evident greatness, a life of manual labour.

Human work comes from persons created in God's image; by enduring the hardship of work in union with Jesus, the carpenter of Nazareth and the one crucified on Calvary, we collaborate in a certain way with the Son of God in his work of redemption.
A just wage is the legitimate fruit of work; to refuse or withhold it can be a grave injustice.
St John Paul II, Laborem Exercens 6 (1981)
Work is for the human person, and not the person for work; the dignity of work comes from the one who works.
Joseph is a working father: from him Jesus learned the value, the dignity and the joy of eating bread that is the fruit of one's own labour.
saints: St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class, in the First Set calendar; in the Latin calendar St Joseph the Worker (optional memorial). May Day. The month of May, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, begins.

1–6 May: the last days of the Resurrection season before the Ascension, in the month of May that our families dedicate to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Sat 1: St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class (May Day). Sun 2: Sixth Sunday of Resurrection; St Athanasius (2 May) gives way to the Sunday. Mon 3: Sts Philip and James, Apostles. Thu 6: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, an important feast and a day of obligation; St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May (verify locally).
2027-05-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you lived for many years as the carpenter's son at Nazareth and worked with human hands. Through the prayers of St Joseph, patron of workers, make holy the labour of our hands and minds. Give work to those who have none, justice to those who are paid unfairly, rest to the weary, and strength to all who toil far from home. Teach us to do everything in your name, giving thanks to the Father through you, and send us from on high the Spirit of wisdom, whom you have promised. Amen. Alleluia!

quick: Genesis: work belonged to God's first plan; sin brought toil and sweat.
Wisdom: Solomon begs for wisdom to labour at his side.
Colossians: do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks.
Matthew: “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” The Son of God worked at Joseph's bench.
2027-05-01.action: Offer your day's work to Christ with a short prayer before you begin, and pray for one person who works far from home.
2027-05-01.question: Do I see my daily work as something I can do in the name of the Lord Jesus?
kidsaint: Joseph was a carpenter in the little village of Nazareth. He made tables, doors and ploughs with wood and tools. Jesus helped him in the workshop, carrying wood and learning to use the hammer and saw. Joseph worked hard so that Jesus and Mary had food and a home. When your father or mother goes to work, remember: Jesus too had a father who worked, and he helped him.
2027-05-01.special: St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class. Fifth Saturday of Resurrection. May Day.
term: The Greek word in the Gospels for Joseph's trade, and for Jesus' own (Mark 6:3): a craftsman or builder working in wood and perhaps stone. It is usually translated ‘carpenter’.

family.explain: The people of Nazareth were surprised when Jesus taught so wisely. ‘Isn't he the carpenter's son?’ they said. Jesus grew up in Joseph's workshop and learned to work hard. St Paul tells us that whatever we do, studying, cooking, cleaning or helping, we can do it for Jesus and say thank you to God.
family.intention: We pray for all who work, for those who have no work, and for our relatives who work far away from home.
family.ask: Ask: “What work can each of us do this week for Jesus, with a happy heart?”

illus: A carpenter in a small town near Thodupuzha kept a picture of St Joseph above his workbench. His son, who had studied engineering, once asked him why he never hurried to finish a job, even when customers were waiting. The old man ran his hand along a door he was making and said, ‘This door will open and close for fifty years. A family will go in and out through it. St Joseph made doors for Nazareth; I think one of them was opened by the hand of Jesus. I cannot do this badly.’ The son said years later that he learned more about Christian work from that answer than from any lecture.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, carpenter of Nazareth, you made holy the work of human hands. As we gather in your name, bless our homes and our labour, through the prayers of St Joseph. Amen. Alleluia!
share: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread (Genesis 3:19). What is tiring and difficult in my work just now?
That she may labor at my side (Wisdom 9:10). Where do I need God's wisdom in my work or studies?
Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus (Colossians 3:17). How can I offer my daily work to him?
Is not this the carpenter’s son? (Matthew 13:55). Where have I failed to see God at work in ordinary people?
pm.resp: St Joseph, patron of workers, pray for us.
interc: For the Church, that she may defend the dignity of every worker.
For those who have no work, and for families who struggle to live on low wages.
For workers who have come to Kerala from other states, and for our own people who work in the Gulf and across the world, that they may be treated justly and kept safe.
For employers and those in authority, that they may pay just wages and protect the weak.
For our families, that like the Holy Family of Nazareth we may work, pray and love together.
pm.close: Father, your Son was known as the carpenter's son and worked with human hands. Through the prayers of St Joseph, make our work holy, our homes peaceful and our hearts open to your Spirit. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, today is May Day, the day many countries honour workers. The Church gives us a worker too: St Joseph, the carpenter of Nazareth, patron of the working class.

The first reading tells us that after the first sin God said to Adam: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Genesis 3:19). But work itself is not a curse. Even before sin, God placed the man in the garden to till it and keep it (Genesis 2:15). Sin brought the thorns, the tiredness and the frustration.

Then the Son of God came and worked with human hands. For many years Jesus worked in Joseph's workshop. In the Gospel the people of Nazareth say, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55). They meant it as an insult. For us it is a joy: our Saviour knows what it is to be tired after a day's work.

Joseph never speaks in the Gospels. He listens to God and obeys. Solomon prays in the second reading for wisdom to labour at his side (Wisdom 9:10). Joseph had that wisdom: quiet, faithful, hard-working. And St Paul tells us, “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17).

Today let us pray for all workers: for those without work, for those paid unjustly, for workers from other states living among us, and for our own children working far from home. And let us offer our own work to the Lord, so that it becomes a prayer. St Joseph, pray for us. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus had a father on earth who was a carpenter: St Joseph. Jesus helped him to make tables and doors.
When you do your homework or help at home, do it for Jesus. Then your work becomes a prayer, just like the work in Joseph's workshop!

intro: Theme: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”
On May Day, with St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class: work in God's plan, toil redeemed by the carpenter's Son, and wisdom that labours at our side.

The Son of God enters our toil.

Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.

points.h: Is not this the carpenter's son?
sub: Joseph who taught a trade to the Son of God.
q: You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be happy, and it shall go well with you.
Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?

concl: The Son of God worked at Joseph's bench, and so every honest work can become holy.
Let us offer our labour in his name, pay and seek just wages, and pray for all who toil.
2027-05-01.resolve: This week, offer your work each morning, thank one worker each day, and pray for those who labour far from home.
